en: To the city of your father the khan
You have carried away
The child I have been cradling.
O Kanykei, my foal,
I have no house built in the city.
The six villains are utter enemies,
And I have no strength to take revenge.
O Kanykei, my foal,
I have lost my twin.
How can I live without loneliness?
If my comfort goes to Bukhara,
O Kanykei, my foal,
Whom shall I take for comfort?
My tiger spoke these words:
‘Until my orphan reaches twelve,
Herd the camels, my noble uncle,
And wait for him,’ he said.
It was a solemn trust;
I shall fulfill his trust.
No support left by the Magnanimous One is here.
O Kanykei, my foal,
Whom shall I take as my support?
From the orphan I took as my support,
From the little one left by my khan,
If it is willed that I be parted thus,
How shall I remain alive?
You will see, my child Kanykei:
When you have gone this way,
I shall not settle along Keng-Kol.
With the six villains and forty swine,
Indeed, Kanykei,
My child, I shall not be as before.
Until twelve years have passed,
My child, I shall herd camels and grieve.
With the dogs who struck down upon you,
When opportunity comes, Kanykei,
I shall keep fighting.
For the only child left by my lord,
I shall care and grieve for twelve years.
If you do not set out in twelve years,
If you do not think to return to Talas,
Then I, Bakai, shall die before my appointed death;
I shall see the face of the other world.
These ownerless herds left in trust—
I shall gather them in a safer place.
O Kanykei, my foal,
If you linger and do not come from Bukhara,
I shall cut short this life.
Fighting wherever I turn,
I shall wreak fierce havoc.
‘My blessing has gone far away,’ I shall say;
I shall treasure you as a gift.
O Kanykei, my foal,
Until you return to Talas,
Until my eyes see the orphan,
I shall not settle along Talas.
By those raven-born dogs,
Until you come to Talas,
I shall not let myself be surrounded.
O Kanykei, my foal,
With the dogs Abyke and Kobosh
I shall remain wherever I survive,
Until the soft dry stalks ripen,
Until the autumn gossamer flies,
I shall fight six months without rest.
When you have settled in Bukhara,
O Kanykei, my foal,
When things are as you wish,
O Kanykei, my foal,
Keep gathering to talk and hear the news.
‘How is he faring?’
Keep asking after your uncle Bakai.
Until you return,
I shall seize their plunder and fight.
With the six villains, Kanykei,
I shall stir up fierce trouble.
If your orphan lives and matures,
If he is notched like white steel,
If he grows into a man and hero,
If he equals the sons of warriors,
O, if God lets him see the Kyrgyz,
O Kanykei, my foal,
Take my migrating camp from Talas.
‘Where is my aged uncle?’ say,
And take my revenge upon the six villains!
Until you set out from Bukhara,
I shall gird my waist tightly.
I shall fortify, Kanykei,
The place where I settle in the heights.
Those seven hundred households are under my hand;
Kanykei, I shall gather my marksmen.
Keep listening for news of me:
I shall wreak fierce havoc on the six villains!
O Kanykei, my foal,
You have been left wandering to Bukhara.
My child, this deed of yours is ill-famed!
Until his age reaches twelve,
O Kanykei, my foal,
My orphan is entrusted to you!
What I saw was a dark night.
From the orphan left by the gray-maned hero,
Parted like this in plain sight,
Was this the day for Bakai to die so?
What is seen today is gone tomorrow.
Alas, this shitty world has deceived us.
My worthless son Baitaylak,
Kanykei and Semetey—
My child, I have no support but you.
I shall know your sacred worth.
Until twelve years have passed,
My child, I shall go on herding camels.
Among the camels, the black riding camel—
I shall guard Jelmaiyan.
Who had pledged his hand to the twelve patrons,
My only one, gone to the other world—
I shall repay Manas's salt.
Who brought slaughter upon so many,
My twin Manas, remain alive!
Father of the people, King Bakai,
To the orphan who fled in distress,
May you never come bringing provisions now!
When the broad world was narrow,
When my gray-maned Manas was alive,
Breaking Ombu and taking booty,
Breaking through its midst and opening a road,
All this world—
When I was trampling across it,
The whole face of the earth—
When I held it in my power,
Why did I not die then?
Making a road through contested places,
Humiliating many peoples,
Going to raid Kokand,
Raiding and taking elephants as booty,
Taking a thousand dark-eyed captives,
The marten-fur hat upon my brow—
When I was making it sway,
Ruling as khan over boundless lands,
When I was living in delight,
When my gray-maned Manas was alive,
Why did I not die then?
The looming city of Great Beijing—
When I was trampling through it,
Chai-Too, where gold was mined—
When I held it in my power,
The black-buttoned kaldai—
When I had him in my grasp,
The kaldai and his Manchus—
When I was beating them,
When the leopard Manas was alive,
Why did I not die then?
Built walls and royal palaces—
When I was taking them,
Those who talked back,
Like ordinary sheep,
When I was splitting them open,
When Bakai ruled as khan,
Beijing with its khakan—
When I was making it bow,
The gold of taxes and tribute—
When I was levying it,
The dark city of Great Beijing—
When I held it in my grasp,
Its lungtungs, its lesser khans—
When I was beating them,
Why did I not die then?
My gray-maned Manas, remain alive;
Bakai, may you never see humiliation!
Lady of a noble lord,
Were you meant to flee in terror?
Unable to find you in the known place,
O Kanykei, my foal,
Was I meant to tear out my beard?
O Kanykei, my foal!”
The noble lord's child
Had fled in terror.
Your valiant uncle Bakai
Had fallen into grievous torment.
That brown two-year-old wether taken for provisions,
His mother Chyiyrdy,
His daughter-in-law Kanykei—
After he had brought it as a gift,
After they had climbed onto the ridge,
That gray-maned uncle's
Wether given as a gift—
Until death, the heart would not forget
The deeds of the six villains in Talas!
Our old uncle Bakai,
The saint upheld by the holy patron,
Kindled their extinguished fire,
Revived their deadened lives,
Gathered what had scattered,
Gladdened their lives, like wooden tubs.
Their scorched hearts recovered.
When they saw King Bakai,
It was as though they saw their khan Manas;
All their sorrow vanished.
When she saw the hero Bakai,
Your fierce mother's
Aching places grew quiet.
Then the woman Kanykei's
Eyes, small as dough pellets, opened.
Into those widows' hands
Your peerless uncle Bakai,
For provisions to drink,
Gave six skins of milk.
To ride away into the distance,
He gave two well-fed horses.
Then, kindling their extinguished fire,
Your tiger, old Bakai,
Revived their deadened lives.
Chyiyrdy was on his right.
The saint, old Bakai,
Thinking and weeping, could not remain still.
Kanykei was on his left.
Upon his looming dark head,
His bloody face was torn.
Unable to muster firm courage,
Your uncle, the leopard Bakai's
Heart burned with sorrow.
Unable to stand for grief,
“May you always remain safe,”
Said King Bakai then,
Giving his hand to his mother Chyiyrdy.
“Wear it on your way to Bukhara,” he said,
And to his child Kanykei
Gave a coat that would keep out the cold.
Sobbing, weeping, embracing them,
Semetey, left by the noble steed,
He entrusted to the two ladies.
“O Kanykei, my foal,
You will reach Temir Khan and settle;
You will make your home beside your father.
Braid the hair upon your back.
The little one you cradle before you,
Give him to your brother Ismail.
Kanykei, my child, keep yourself apart;
Turn your thoughts another way.
Until your child grows and mounts a horse,
Do not dress him in your arrow-proof coat.
That Manas, gone to the other world,
Is his father, my foal, do not let him know.
When his age reaches twelve,
Send him to the Kyrgyz, to Talas.
Have the Quran recited, Kanykei,
For my companion, Sultan Manas.
When his age reaches twelve,
I shall scout the heights of the cliffs.
If Bakai does not die of suffering,
If he does not see the Last Judgment,
The gift left by the mighty warrior
I shall take as my companion.
Teaching him the things he does not know,
I, knowledgeable old Bakai,
Shall make him understand what he has not grasped.
I, falcon-like old Bakai,
